solution:
Section 13.2.2 gives the rule used throughout: a secondary or tertiary amine is named as an N-substituted derivative of a primary amine, the LARGEST alkyl group attached to nitrogen being taken as the parent alkane and the others as N-substituents, listed alphabetically.

a. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-N(CH_3)-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\). The three groups on nitrogen are ethyl, methyl and propyl; the largest is propyl, so the parent is propan-1-amine, and the other two become N-ethyl and N-methyl. The name is N-Ethyl-N-methylpropan-1-amine. (Table 13.2 lists the same compound skeleton under tertiary amines with exactly this IUPAC name.)

b. \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\). Only one group is attached to nitrogen, so this is a primary amine. Numbering the chain from the carbon bearing the amino group gives a four-carbon parent, butan-1-amine, carrying two methyl groups on C-3. The name is 3,3-Dimethylbutan-1-amine.

c. \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(CH_3)-NH-CH_2-CH_3}\). The two groups on nitrogen are ethyl and propan-2-yl (isopropyl); the larger is the three-carbon one, so the parent is propan-2-amine, with the ethyl group as the N-substituent. The name is N-Ethylpropan-2-amine.

WHAT AMINES ARE. The chapter opens by defining them: 'Amines are nitrogen containing organic compounds having basic character.' Structurally (section 13.1) they are obtained by replacing one, two or three of the hydrogen atoms of an ammonia molecule by alkyl or aryl groups. They occur widely in nature - in proteins, vitamins, hormones and plant products such as nicotine.

HOW THEY ARE CLASSIFIED. The chapter classifies them in three ways.

1. By the NUMBER of alkyl or aryl groups bonded directly to nitrogen (Table 13.1):

| Type | Functional group | Formula | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary, \(1^\circ\) | amino | \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) | \(\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH_2}\), ethylamine |
| Secondary, \(2^\circ\) | imino | \(\mathrm{{>}NH}\) | \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2NH}\), dimethylamine |
| Tertiary, \(3^\circ\) | tertiary nitrogen | \(\mathrm{{\gg}N}\) | \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\), trimethylamine |

2. Secondary and tertiary amines are further divided into SIMPLE (symmetrical) amines, in which all the alkyl or aryl groups on nitrogen are the same, and MIXED (unsymmetrical) amines, in which they differ.

3. By the NATURE of the groups attached to nitrogen, amines fall into two major classes: ALIPHATIC amines, in which nitrogen carries alkyl groups, and AROMATIC amines (arylamines), in which it is bonded directly to an aromatic ring, aniline being the parent.

The chapter's 'Remember...' box stresses that the first classification counts groups on the NITROGEN, not the nature of the carbon atom carrying the functional group - so isopropylamine is a primary amine even though isopropyl alcohol is a secondary alcohol.

a. \(\mathrm{H_2N-(CH_2)_6-NH_2}\) is Hexane-1,6-diamine. Section 13.2.2 states that when two or more amino groups are present the prefix 'di-' is used with proper locants and the ending 'e' of the parent alkane is RETAINED; Table 13.2 lists this exact compound (common name hexamethylenediamine) with this IUPAC name.

b. The benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) and two \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) groups, one ortho and one para to the amino group, is 2,4-Dimethylaniline (equivalently 2,4-dimethylbenzenamine). Table 13.2 names the singly methylated analogue p-toluidine as 4-Methylaniline, so the ring methyls are cited as locants plus 'methyl' on the parent aniline; here the amino carbon is C-1 and the two methyls are on C-2 and C-4.

c. The benzene ring carrying two \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) groups para to one another is Benzene-1,4-diamine (also written 1,4-diaminobenzene; its common name is p-phenylenediamine). The two amino groups are equivalent, so neither can be the parent-defining one and the compound is named as a diamine of benzene, in the same way ethylenediamine is named ethane-1,2-diamine in Table 13.2.

Each starting material needs a different method, because the carbon count differs.

a. From ACETONITRILE \(\mathrm{CH_3-C}\equiv\mathrm{N}\) (2 carbon atoms, but only one in the chain apart from the nitrile carbon). Section 13.3.3, the Mendius reduction, adds two hydrogens to the nitrile carbon:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-C}\equiv\mathrm{N} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow[\text{or}\ \mathrm{LiAlH_4}]{\mathrm{Na/C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\)

b. From NITROETHANE \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NO_2}\) (2 carbon atoms). Section 13.3.2, reduction of a nitrocompound by a metal-acid mixture, keeps the carbon count unchanged:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NO_2} + 6[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn/HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

c. From PROPIONAMIDE \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CO-NH_2}\) (3 carbon atoms). Here the product has one carbon FEWER than the amide, so this is a step-down and the method required is Hofmann bromamide degradation (section 13.3.6), not the reduction of amides:

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CO-NH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{K_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Note the contrast with section 13.3.4: reducing propionamide with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) would preserve all three carbons and give propylamine, not ethanamine. It is the loss of the carbonyl carbon in Hofmann degradation that makes the amide route work here.

Acetic anhydride is an acylating agent, and section 13.6.4 states that 'aliphatic and aromatic primary and secondary amines undergo acylation reaction. These amines contain replaceable hydrogen atoms (positively polarised H) on the nitrogen atom. These hydrogen atoms are replaced by acyl groups such as acetyl group', giving an acetyl derivative of the amine, that is, an amide. The reaction is carried out in the presence of a strong base such as pyridine, which neutralises the acid produced.

ETHYLAMINE (primary, two hydrogens on nitrogen) is acetylated:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH_2} + \mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{pyridine}} \mathrm{C_2H_5-NH-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

The product is N-ethylethanamide (N-ethylacetamide).

DIETHYLAMINE (secondary, one hydrogen on nitrogen) is likewise acetylated, at its single N-H:

\(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH} + \mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O} \xrightarrow{\text{pyridine}} \mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2N-CO-CH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

The product is N,N-diethylethanamide (N,N-diethylacetamide).

TRIETHYLAMINE (tertiary) has NO hydrogen on nitrogen - the chapter's 'Can you tell ?' box makes exactly this point - so there is nothing for the acetyl group to replace and no acylation occurs. Triethylamine gives no acetyl derivative with acetic anhydride.

In each case where reaction does occur the amide formed is less basic than the parent amine, because the nitrogen lone pair is drawn into the acetyl group; this is the very effect the chapter uses to protect the amino group of aniline before bromination and nitration.

[Textbook misprint: block 4 of the Exercises skips the label "vi" altogether — the printed items run i, ii, iii, iv, v, vii, viii, so the block contains SEVEN questions and not eight. Nothing is missing from the page between item v and this one; only the numeral is. The book's own labels are kept here rather than renumbered.]

Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulfonyl chloride \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\) (section 13.8). Each amine is shaken with the reagent and the mixture is then treated with aqueous NaOH; the three behave differently.

ETHYLAMINE (primary). It reacts to give N-ethylbenzene sulfonamide:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl} + \mathrm{H_2N-C_2H_5} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2-NH-C_2H_5} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

One hydrogen is left on the nitrogen, and the chapter states that this hydrogen 'is strongly acidic. Hence it is soluble in alkali.' So the product DISSOLVES in aqueous NaOH, giving a clear solution.

DIETHYLAMINE (secondary). It also reacts, giving N,N-diethylbenzene sulfonamide:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl} + \mathrm{HN(C_2H_5)_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2-N(C_2H_5)_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Of this product the chapter says it 'does not contain any H-atom attached to nitrogen atom. Hence it is not acidic and does not dissolve in alkali.' So a precipitate forms and it stays INSOLUBLE in aqueous NaOH.

TRIETHYLAMINE (tertiary). It has no hydrogen on nitrogen, so there is no N-H for the sulfonyl group to replace and NO REACTION takes place; the amine simply remains unchanged and separates out, undissolved in the alkali.

The three outcomes - a product soluble in alkali, a product insoluble in alkali, and no reaction at all - distinguish the primary, secondary and tertiary amine respectively. [Note: the chapter states the primary and secondary cases explicitly; for the tertiary case it poses the reason as a 'Can you tell ?' question - 'Why do tertiary amines not react with benzene sulfonyl chloride ?' - rather than writing it out.]

a. ANILINE INTO p-NITROANILINE. Direct nitration is not the answer: section 13.9(b) records that it 'yields a mixture of ortho, meta and para nitroanilines' - 51% para, 47% meta and 2% ortho - because in the acidic nitrating medium the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group is protonated to \(\mathrm{-NH_3^{\oplus}}\), which is meta-directing and deactivating, so a considerable amount of m-nitroaniline is formed. The chapter's own remedy is to protect the amino group first: 'to get p-nitroaniline as major product, \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group is first protected by acetylation, nitration is carried out and then amide is hydrolysed.'

Aniline \(\xrightarrow[\text{pyridine}]{\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}}\) acetanilide \(\xrightarrow[288\ \mathrm{K}]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3} + \text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}}\) p-nitroacetanilide \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\ \text{or}\ \mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}}\) p-nitroaniline

b. ANILINE INTO SULPHANILIC ACID. Section 13.9(c): 'Aniline reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to form anilinium hydrogen sulfate which on heating with sulfuric acid at 453-473 K produces p-aminobenzene sulfonic acid (sulfanilic acid) as major product.'

Aniline \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2SO_4}}\) anilinium hydrogensulfate \(\xrightarrow{453\text{-}473\ \mathrm{K}}\) sulfanilic acid

Sulfanilic acid is \(\mathrm{p\text{-}H_2N-C_6H_4-SO_3H}\). The chapter adds that it does not in fact exist in that neutral form: it exists as a salt called a dipolar ion or ZWITTER ION, \(\mathrm{p\text{-}{}^{\oplus}H_3N-C_6H_4-SO_3^{\ominus}}\), produced by reaction between the acidic group and the basic group present in the same molecule.
